title: The Diagram That Spoke for the Soldiers
subtitle: In the 1850s a nurse turned thousands of deaths into one picture. The lesson for speakers is what she did with the numbers before she drew it.

card.essence: A hospital, a pamphlet and a coloured diagram. Why a number alone means nothing, and the three moves that give it a meaning in speech.

intention: you'll see why exact figures slip past listeners, build a round-compare-mean habit for spoken numbers, and use it to say any figure so that it is remembered.
warmup: Think of a number you were told recently that you can still remember. What made it stick?
When someone reads out a figure like 4,903 or 62.4 per cent, what do you do with it as a listener?
Do you prefer to hear exact numbers or round ones? Does it depend on who is speaking?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: Within a month the death rate had plummeted, from nearly half to a fraction of that figure.
items.meaning: plummet — to fall very fast and by a large amount. The opposite is soar.

items.sent: The difference between the two samples was so small that it was negligible.
items.meaning: negligible — so small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.

items.sent: A disproportionate number of the deaths came from one cause.
items.meaning: disproportionate — too large or too small in comparison with something else. The noun is disproportion.

items.sent: To judge whether a change is big, you first need a baseline: where things stood before.
items.meaning: baseline — a starting figure used for comparison, so that you can tell how much something has changed.

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: rule of thumb · ballpark figure · at a glance. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means a rough estimate, good enough to start a discussion?
items.meaning: ballpark figure — Can you give me a ballpark figure for the cost? The idea comes from baseball: you are somewhere in the stadium.

items.sent: Which term means immediately, without needing to study something carefully?
items.meaning: at a glance — A good chart lets you see the trend at a glance.

items.sent: Which term means a simple practical guide based on experience, not on exact calculation?
items.meaning: rule of thumb — As a rule of thumb, a meeting should never run longer than the number of people in it times ten minutes.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: ___ a figure  ·  ___ a price  ·  ___ a source
items.meaning: quote — to repeat the exact words or numbers that someone else gave, or to state a price.

items.sent: spot the ___  ·  follow the ___  ·  reverse the ___
items.meaning: trend — the general direction in which something is changing over time.

items.sent: a narrow ___  ·  a profit ___  ·  a ___ of error
items.meaning: margin — the amount by which something is won, gained or allowed, or the difference between two figures.

vocab_use: Tell me about a trend you have noticed lately. What is the baseline you are comparing it with?
Give me a ballpark figure for something you do not know exactly, such as the number of people in your street or the cost of your commute.
Describe something you can understand at a glance and something that takes you a long time to understand. What is different about them?

story.heading: Part 1 — The hospital at Scutari
paras: In 1854, Britain was at war with Russia in the Crimea. Thousands of British soldiers were sick or wounded, and the army sent them to a huge hospital at Scutari, across the water from Constantinople. Florence Nightingale, a nurse from a wealthy English family, arrived there with a group of other nurses.

The hospital was overcrowded and dirty. Many of the men who arrived with wounds or fevers died there of diseases they caught inside the building. By the figures she used, as many as four in ten of the men in that hospital were dying in the early months of 1855.

In March 1855, a government sanitary commission arrived to inspect the buildings. It had sewers cleared and ventilation improved. Soon afterwards, the death rate at the hospital fell to a small fraction of what it had been.
checks: Where was Nightingale working, and why?
Roughly what share of the men in the hospital were dying in early 1855?
What did the sanitary commission change?
answers: At the hospital in Scutari, treating British soldiers during the Crimean War.
As many as four in ten, according to the figures she used.
It had the sewers cleared and the ventilation improved, after which the death rate fell sharply.
story.discuss: A figure like 'four in ten' is easy to hear and hard to forget. How would the same fact sound if the speaker said 'forty-two point three per cent'?

story.heading: Part 2 — The comparison
paras: After the war, Nightingale went back to England and worked on a government inquiry into the health of the army. She was a gifted mathematician, and she gathered the army's records and worked through them herself. She then did something that made the figures meaningful: she compared them with the death rates for civilian men of the same age, using tables compiled by the statistician William Farr.

The comparison showed that soldiers in peacetime were dying at a much higher rate than civilians. It also showed that, in the Crimean War, far more soldiers had died from disease than from their wounds. Neither fact was obvious from the raw numbers alone. Each needed a baseline.
This was the move that made her case. A number on its own tells the listener little. A number next to another number tells them how big, how bad and how different.
checks: What did Nightingale compare the army's death rates with?
What did the comparison show about peacetime?
What did it show about the Crimean War?
answers: The death rates for civilian men of the same age, using tables compiled by William Farr.
That soldiers in peacetime were dying at a much higher rate than civilians.
That far more soldiers died of disease than of their wounds.
story.discuss: She chose civilian men as her baseline. What would have happened to her argument if she had chosen a different group? How do you check that a comparison is fair?

story.heading: Part 3 — The rose
paras: In 1858 Nightingale published a long report that included a coloured diagram, now called her rose diagram. Each wedge showed a month of the war, and the size of the wedge showed how many soldiers died. Blue showed deaths from disease, red showed deaths from wounds, and black showed other causes.
The diagram was designed for readers who would never read tables of figures: politicians and officials who had the power to change things. At a glance, the blue wedges were far bigger than the red.

The lesson for a speaker is that she did not simply show the figure. She rounded it into an idea, compared it with something, and told the reader what it meant. A listener has no diagram. The rounded number, the comparison and the meaning have to be said aloud, in that order.
checks: What did the size of each wedge show?
What did the colours blue and red stand for?
Who was the diagram designed for, and why?
answers: How many soldiers died in each month of the war.
Blue showed deaths from disease; red showed deaths from wounds.
Politicians and officials who would not read tables of figures, but who could see the pattern at a glance.
story.discuss: A speaker has no diagram, only words. How could you make a listener 'see' a figure in the way the blue wedges made readers see it?

tool_tab.lead: Nightingale made figures visible with colour. A speaker has to make them audible. Statisticians call it being numerate; communicators call it making a number mean something. The tool below has three moves, in order, and one rule: the exact figure waits until somebody asks for it.
how: Round it. Turn the exact figure into a number the ear can hold: nearly a third, just over four in ten, roughly double. Exact figures sound precise but are forgotten at once.
Compare it. Give the listener a baseline: compared with last year…, twice the national average, the highest in ten years. A number with no comparison cannot be judged.
Mean it. Say what it tells us: which means…, in other words…. The meaning is why the number matters.
Keep the exact figure ready. If someone asks, give it at once: Precisely, it was 26.3 per cent. You get credit for being exact because you did not lead with it.

sort.intro: These sentences are all ways of saying a figure. Which step of the tool does each one belong to? Choose, then check.

items.why: every digit given; accurate, but it is hard to hold in the ear.

items.text: Revenue was about three and a half million.
items.why: a number the listener can remember, with about signalling that it is approximate.

items.text: That is nearly double what we made two years ago.
items.why: it gives the figure a baseline, so the listener can judge its size.

items.text: In other words, we have finally covered our costs.
items.why: in other words says what the figures amount to.

items.text: Just over a quarter of staff said they would leave.
items.why: a fraction instead of a percentage, with just over to show it is approximate.
a figure with a decimal; keep it for when someone asks.

items.text: That is the highest figure in our sector.
items.why: it compares one figure with all the others in the group.

items.text: Which means we are losing about one person a week.
items.why: it turns the figure into something concrete that the listener can picture.

items.text: Roughly one in three trains arrived late.
items.why: one in three is much easier to hold in the ear than a percentage with decimals.

items.text: Late trains rose from 18.4 per cent to 33.1 per cent.
items.why: two exact figures; accurate, but nearly impossible to remember after one hearing.

breaks: When precision matters. In medicine, law and accounting, the exact number is the message. Drug doses, deadlines and legal limits must be stated in full.
When rounding changes the story. Rounding 29 per cent to nearly a third is fair; rounding 41 per cent to about half is not. Round only as far as the truth allows.
When the comparison is chosen to flatter you. Comparing this month with the worst month of last year tells the listener nothing. Pick a baseline the listener would accept as fair.
discuss: Which is harder for you: rounding a number, finding a fair comparison, or saying what it means? Why?
Have you ever been persuaded by a number that turned out to be misleading? What had the speaker done?

grammar.name: Saying numbers naturally
grammar.lead: Spoken numbers use a different grammar from written ones. The patterns below let you round, compare and describe change in language that sounds natural.
notes: Approximators: about, roughly, around, in the region of for either side; nearly, almost, just under for slightly below; just over, a little more than for slightly above. Nearly a third is a little less than 33 per cent; just over a third is a little more.
Fractions and ratios: a quarter, a third, two thirds, three quarters; one in four, nine out of ten. Multiples: twice as many as, three times higher than, has doubled / tripled / halved.

Change: by gives the difference (rose by 12 per cent), to gives the new level (rose to 56 million), from…to gives both (rose from 50 to 56 million), and of follows the noun (an increase of nine per cent).

exercises.heading: By, to, from, of
exercises.intro: Use each word from the box once: by · to · from · of.
items: 1. Profits rose ___ twelve per cent, from 50 to 56 million.
2. Unemployment has fallen ___ 6.1 per cent, its lowest level in a decade.
3. Costs have gone up ___ 40 to 52 thousand a month.
4. There has been an increase ___ nine per cent in sick leave.
answers: 1. by — gives the size of the change.
3. from — gives the starting level; to 52 thousand completes it.

exercises.heading: Say the change
exercises.intro: Choose the word or phrase that matches the arithmetic.
items: 1. Applications rose from 200 to 600, so they have ___ (tripled / doubled).
2. Out of 40 staff, 10 left, so ___ (a quarter / a third) of them left.
3. A price went from £50 to £100, so it is ___ (half / twice) as expensive as before.
4. The cost fell from £90 to £60, a fall of ___ (a third / a half).
5. Of 500 customers, 495 said yes, so ___ (nearly all / about half) of them did.
answers: 5. nearly all — 495 out of 500 is 99 per cent.

grammar.closing: Now say one number from this week — a price, a time, a distance, a count — in a rounded form, with a comparison.

speak.intro: Round it, compare it, give it a meaning, then speak. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “Nearly a…” · “Just over…” · “That is twice…” · “Compared with…” · “In other words…” · “Precisely, it was…”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Say it so it sticks
paras: Say each of these as you would to a busy listener: 4,903 out of 14,820 customers / 62.4 per cent of respondents / £2,198,400 in revenue / unemployment moving from 0.9 to 3.1 per cent. Round each one, compare it with something, and say what it means.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Choose a statistic
paras: Pick a figure you know from work, study or the news. Give it in three moves: rounded, compared, meaning. Then say what the exact figure would be, if someone asked.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The story in sixty seconds
paras: Tell the story of Nightingale and the rose diagram in sixty seconds, starting with the meaning: what does it show about speaking? Use at least two rounded numbers and one comparison.

final: Is it dishonest to round a number? Where would you draw the line?
How can a speaker tell a fair comparison from a flattering one? What would you check?
In your field, which number do people most often get wrong or misunderstand?
From memory: explain the three moves in four sentences, using round, compare, baseline and in other words.

practice.intro: One page of figures to say aloud. Pick a figure, take ten seconds to decide how you will round it, compare it and give it a meaning, and then say it in twenty seconds.
steps: Ten seconds: round it, find a baseline, decide the meaning.
Twenty seconds: the rounded number first, then the comparison, then which means…
Stop and keep the exact figure ready for when someone asks.

groups.title: Business
groups.intro: The listener is a busy manager.
questions: Staff turnover was 26.3 per cent this year and 14.1 per cent last year.
Revenue was £3,412,806, up from £1,764,200 two years ago.
Customer satisfaction scored 7.2 out of 10 in March and 6.1 in June.
Of 14,820 customers, 4,903 bought again within a year.
The company's market share is 18.7 per cent, and the next competitor's is 17.9.

groups.title: Health
groups.intro: A number a patient or a colleague needs to understand.
questions: Waiting times rose from 1 hour 52 minutes to 4 hours 48 minutes.
Out of 1,000 patients, 83 had a complication.
The treatment reduces the risk from 2.1 per cent to 1.4 per cent.
Ninety-six per cent of beds were occupied last winter.
The test is accurate in 91 out of 100 cases.

groups.title: Money and prices
groups.intro: The listener thinks in pounds and cents.
questions: Prices rose by 6.4 per cent while wages rose by 3.1 per cent.
The average rent is £1,486 a month and the average salary is £3,720 after tax.
A coffee used to cost £1.80 and now costs £3.40.
Our energy bill rose from £162 to £331 a month.
Interest on the loan will be £12,480 on a loan of £35,000.

groups.title: Cities and the world
groups.intro: Big numbers need a human scale.
questions: A city of 1.2 million is losing 9,800 residents a year.
A new airline carried 4.4 million passengers last year and 2.2 million five years ago.
Seventy-one per cent of the planet's surface is water.
A country has 67.3 million people, and 84 per cent of them live in towns.
The new line carries 31,000 passengers an hour in each direction.

groups.title: Everyday life
groups.intro: A number you meet in ordinary conversation.
questions: The average person checks their phone 96 times a day.
It takes 23 minutes on average to get back to a task after being interrupted.
Forty-eight per cent of the people surveyed read no books last year.
My commute takes 1 hour 17 minutes each way.
I spend £412 a month on food and £640 on rent.

models.q: Staff turnover was 26.3 per cent this year and 14.1 per cent last year.
parts: Rounded
More than one person in four left this year.
Compared
That is almost double last year's figure, when it was about one in seven.
Meaning
In other words, we are replacing a quarter of the department every year.

models.q: Out of 1,000 patients, 83 had a complication.
parts: Rounded
Roughly one patient in twelve had a complication.
Compared
That is higher than the one in twenty that we expect.
Meaning
Which means we should look at what changed in the way we do the procedure.

models.q: A coffee used to cost £1.80 and now costs £3.40.
parts: Rounded
A coffee now costs nearly double what it used to.
Compared
Prices in general have risen far less, by a fifth or so over the same years.
Meaning
So coffee has become a luxury in a way that bread and milk have not.

models.q: The average rent is £1,486 a month and the average salary is £3,720 after tax.
parts: Rounded
The average rent takes about forty per cent of the average salary.
Compared
A rule of thumb says rent should be around a third, so this is well above the guide.
Meaning
In other words, there is not much left over for saving.

models.q: The treatment reduces the risk from 2.1 per cent to 1.4 per cent.
parts: Rounded
It lowers the risk from about two in a hundred to about one and a half in a hundred.
Compared
That is a fall of roughly a third, but only about seven in a thousand patients.
Meaning
So it matters most for people who are already at high risk.

models.q: My commute takes 1 hour 17 minutes each way.
parts: Rounded
I spend about two and a half hours a day travelling.
Compared
That is nearly thirteen hours a week, which is more than two full days a month.
Meaning
In other words, it is like having a second part-time job that I do not get paid for.

harder: Shorter: say the figure with a comparison in a single sentence.
Interrupted: your partner says Can you be more exact? after you round. Give the exact figure at once, without apologising.
Opposite comparison: choose a different baseline that makes the same figure look smaller. Which baseline is fairer, and why?
For a different listener: say the figure to an expert, to a customer, and to a child. The number stays the same; the comparison changes.
Without numbers: describe the same fact using only words such as most, few, about half, almost none. What do you lose?
